newsitem.title: GERMANY: German conservatives bury coalition woes.
newsitem.headline: German conservatives bury coalition woes.

text.p: Germany's governing Christian Democrats (CDU) buried a bitter dispute with their coalition partners on Thursday over budget and tax cuts, and vowed to press on with stalled fiscal reform.
Rather than sniping at liberal coalition partners over the cuts, CDU leaders aimed heavy fire on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) for the first time in weeks.
"The SPD is the biggest obstacle there is to investment in Germany," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told German Radio.
"With their voting majority in the upper house of parliament, they are blocking the decisions we need to make."

Many of the coalition's legislative initiatives aimed at cutting the high 10 percent unemployment rate and reducing barriers to investment in Germany have been vetoed by the SPD-controlled upper house.
Political squabbling has centred on the budget for 1997, key year for deciding the starting line-up of countries joining in European economic and monetary union.

Faced with falling tax revenues and rising unemployment outlays, Finance Minister Theo Waigel has fought a bruising personal battle to slash federal spending and hold the 1997 government deficit comfortably below the three percent of economic output targeted in the EU's Maastricht Treaty.
CDU General Secretary Peter Hintze said the party had put its recent battles with coalition partner, the Free Democrats (FDP) behind it and would concentrate efforts on the opposition.
His remarks came as a new opinion poll showed the SPD moving alongside the alliance of the CDU and its Bavarian sister party Christian Social Union (CSU).
The Forsa research institute said both parties were equal at 39.0 percent, with the SPD gaining one point since a similar poll two weeks ago.

The FDP were down one point at 5.0 percent while the environmentalist Greens, a likely coalition partner for the SPD, were steady at 10 percent. The reform communist PDS were down two points at four percent.
Hintze said the CDU and CSU remained committed to maintaining the coalition with the FDP until the next elections in 1998.
"The relationships in the coalition are back in good shape after the series of minor irritations in recent weeks," Hintze told a group of journalists on Thursday.

Those "minor irritations" over budget cuts threatened to end the 14-year coalition government when Chancellor Helmut Kohl erupted at one contentious meeting last week with a threat to resign and bring the government down.

But a Kohl ally said the chancellor's resignation threat was not serious. Friedrich Zimmermann, a former interior minister in Kohl's cabinet, said the chancellor is at his best when the pressure is on.
"Whenever he has his back to the wall and whenever it starts to hit the fan, he is better at staying up on his feet than any German politician I have ever seen," Zimmermann told the Bild daily.
